scenes.tts: Why does the R shape hold oxygen better than T? The answer starts with a movement smaller than an atom.
scenes.visual: Title fades. Zoom from a hemoglobin molecule into one heme. On screen: Why does R grip harder?
scenes.narration: Why does the R shape hold oxygen better than T? The answer starts with a movement smaller than an atom.

scenes.tts: Hemoglobin is four chains, two alpha and two beta. They pair up as two alpha-beta dimers.
scenes.caption: Hemoglobin is four chains, two α and two β. They pair up as two αβ dimers.
scenes.visual: Tetramer drawn as two α chains and two β chains, grouped into two αβ dimers.
scenes.narration: Hemoglobin is four chains, two α and two β. They pair up as two αβ dimers.

scenes.tts: Each chain cradles one heme. Heme is a ring, protoporphyrin nine, with an iron at its center.
scenes.caption: Each chain cradles one heme. Heme is a ring, protoporphyrin IX, with an iron at its center.
scenes.visual: Close-up of heme: flat porphyrin ring with an iron atom in the middle.
scenes.narration: Each chain cradles one heme. Heme is a ring, protoporphyrin IX, with an iron at its center.

scenes.tts: The iron makes four bonds to the ring's nitrogens. A fifth bond goes to a histidine below, the proximal histidine.
scenes.visual: Four bonds from Fe to the ring nitrogens light up; then a fifth to a histidine below, labelled proximal His.
scenes.narration: The iron makes four bonds to the ring's nitrogens. A fifth bond goes to a histidine below, the proximal histidine.

scenes.tts: The sixth site is saved for oxygen. Across the pocket sits the distal histidine, which hydrogen-bonds to bound oxygen.
scenes.visual: O₂ binds above the iron at an angle; a distal His above it forms a dashed hydrogen bond.
scenes.narration: The sixth site is saved for oxygen. Across the pocket sits the distal histidine, which hydrogen-bonds to bound oxygen.

scenes.tts: The iron must stay in its plus-two form. Oxidized, it becomes methemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen at all.
scenes.visual: Label Fe²⁺ (works). A ghost Fe³⁺ marked methemoglobin, no O₂.
scenes.narration: The iron must stay in its plus-two form. Oxidized, it becomes methemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen at all.

scenes.tts: Step one. In T, the iron is high-spin and slightly too big for the ring's hole. It sits about zero point four angstroms below the ring, toward the histidine.
scenes.caption: Step one. In T, the iron is high-spin and slightly too big for the ring's hole. It sits about 0.4 Å below the ring, toward the histidine.
scenes.visual: Side view of the heme: iron sitting just below the plane, on the proximal histidine's side (oxygen binds on the top face). Scale bar: 0.4 Å, beside a water molecule for size. Step 1 of 4.
scenes.narration: Step one. In T, the iron is high-spin and slightly too big for the ring's hole. It sits about 0.4 Å below the ring, toward the histidine.

scenes.tts: That is about a seventh of the width of a water molecule.
scenes.visual: The 0.4 Å gap beside a water molecule, about one seventh of its width.
scenes.narration: That is about a seventh of the width of a water molecule.

scenes.tts: When oxygen binds, the iron turns low-spin, shrinks, and rises into the plane.
scenes.visual: O₂ binds on top; the iron shrinks and rises into the ring's plane.
scenes.narration: When oxygen binds, the iron turns low-spin, shrinks, and rises into the plane.

scenes.tts: Step two. The iron is bonded to the proximal histidine, so the histidine follows it.
scenes.visual: The proximal histidine is pulled toward the ring. Step 2 of 4.
scenes.narration: Step two. The iron is bonded to the proximal histidine, so the histidine follows it.

scenes.tts: Step three. That histidine sits on a helix, the F helix. The helix shifts and presses on the neighboring subunit.
scenes.visual: The F helix, drawn as a ribbon carrying the histidine, shifts and pushes against the next subunit. Step 3 of 4.
scenes.narration: Step three. That histidine sits on a helix, the F helix. The helix shifts and presses on the neighboring subunit.

scenes.tts: Step four. In Max Perutz's classic account, this is levered into a rotation of one dimer against the other, about fifteen degrees.
scenes.caption: Step four. In Max Perutz's classic account, this is levered into a rotation of one dimer against the other, about 15°.
scenes.visual: One αβ dimer rotates against the other by about 15°. Step 4 of 4.
scenes.narration: Step four. In Max Perutz's classic account, this is levered into a rotation of one dimer against the other, about 15°.

scenes.tts: The salt bridges that held T break, and the molecule moves toward R.
scenes.visual: Salt-bridge links between subunits snap; label changes from T to R.
scenes.narration: The salt bridges that held T break, and the molecule moves toward R.

scenes.tts: In T, those salt bridges resist this chain of movements. That is why a heme in T binds oxygen weakly.
scenes.visual: In the T outline, the salt-bridge links hold the helix back; the iron struggles to drop. Label: T resists, so binding is weaker.
scenes.narration: In T, those salt bridges resist this chain of movements. That is why a heme in T binds oxygen weakly.

scenes.tts: Later work shows the coupling is looser than a gear train. Each iron shift raises the odds of the switch rather than forcing it.
scenes.visual: A gear train fades out; an odds dial for R ticks up a notch with each iron drop.
scenes.narration: Later work shows the coupling is looser than a gear train. Each iron shift raises the odds of the switch rather than forcing it.

scenes.tts: That fits the two-shape picture. Each oxygen bound makes R more likely, not certain.
scenes.visual: Population bar of the earlier chapter, nudging toward R with each oxygen.
scenes.narration: That fits the two-shape picture. Each oxygen bound makes R more likely, not certain.

scenes.tts: Perutz saw the two end points by solving deoxy and oxy hemoglobin side by side.
scenes.visual: Morph between the deoxy structure (PDB 2HHB, T) and the oxy structure (PDB 1HHO, R).
scenes.narration: Perutz saw the two end points by solving deoxy and oxy hemoglobin side by side.

scenes.tts: Do all four subunits switch together, or one at a time? Real hemoglobin fits neither textbook model perfectly.
scenes.visual: Two cartoons: all four flip together (concerted) versus one at a time (sequential). Question mark between.
scenes.narration: Do all four subunits switch together, or one at a time? Real hemoglobin fits neither textbook model perfectly.

scenes.tts: Its overall switch looks concerted. But each subunit's own shape also shifts as it binds.
scenes.visual: The tetramer flips as a whole; inside it, each subunit also flexes slightly as it binds.
scenes.narration: Its overall switch looks concerted. But each subunit's own shape also shifts as it binds.

scenes.tts: A tiny shift at one iron, levered through a helix, raises the odds that the whole molecule turns to R.
scenes.visual: End card. LINE: A sub-ångström iron drop, levered through the F helix, raises the odds of R.
scenes.narration: A tiny shift at one iron, levered through a helix, raises the odds that the whole molecule turns to R.

scenes.visual: End card. LINE: A sub-ångström iron drop, levered through the F helix, raises the odds of R.
